supported_claims.text: 頁 is analyzed as a pictograph of a kneeling person with the head emphasized; oracle-bone examples are interpreted with the meanings “pig’s head” and “bowing the head.”
The pictograph’s visible parts are pictorial: 首 represents the emphasized head, and 卩 the kneeling person. This analysis concerns the traditional graph 頁, not the simplified graph 页.

頁 and 首 are described as graphic variants of the same head pictograph, distinguished by whether the body is drawn. This is a graphic relationship, not evidence that modern 页 contains those same parts.

Reported graphic history includes oracle-bone forms that may show or omit hair, a Western Zhou bronze form with hair, Warring States forms in which hair is often distorted into 止, and a small-seal form omitting hair. The curated seal image is a modern drawing, not an ancient artifact image.

The received Shuowen account glosses 頁 as “head” and analyzes it as 𦣻 plus 几; the database analysis instead describes head-plus-body pictography, and a later textual-critical note disputes the received component wording. These are distinct accounts, not settled proof of one exact ancient split.

頁 was used as a common or popular written form for 葉 in the paper, sheet, or page sense. This is a borrowing or spelling substitution for a different word, not a demonstrated semantic development from “head”; the old sound match is not independently established here.

The dossier records yè for the page-use reading and xié for the head reading, and reports 胡結切 for the head reading by the Eastern Han at the latest. These readings do not establish the historical name of the depicted object or the sound mechanism behind the 葉 spelling.

disagreements.text: The pictographic analysis describes 頁 as 卩 plus 首, a kneeling person with the head emphasized; the received Shuowen text instead says 𦣻 plus 几. The Shuowen wording is text-critically disputed, so these component accounts should remain separate.

One account describes 页 as derived from the cursive script of 頁, while another says it is the simplified form of 頁. The dossier does not resolve the specific graphic path; it supports treating 页 as the simplified counterpart, without assigning the traditional graph’s internal component analysis to it.

limitations.text: The supplied evidence gives no independently verified earliest dated attestation for 頁 used in the 葉 paper/page sense, nor a dated sequence of later extensions such as page to leaf.

The broad sound resemblance proposed for borrowing 頁 to write 葉 is not independently demonstrated by a sourced comparison of the relevant historical readings. The recorded readings and reconstructed forms must not be conflated or used to assert that the depicted head was called by the pronoun’s reading.

The cited oracle-bone and bronze forms and their interpretations are reported through database descriptions; the artifact images were not independently inspected. The isolated bronze phrase 頁手 is considered possibly abbreviated or erroneous.

The supplied record does not establish a distinct internal component split for modern 页. The relationship of the whole simplified graph to 頁 does not license carrying over the traditional graph’s components as current components.
The reported Japanese readings and modern Mandarin entries are metadata, not evidence for the graph’s origin or the historical sound relation behind the borrowing.
